This region already has connectors named Portage, Rosetta and Parallax. Each keeps a notebook of their own, as you will; you are joining them, not replacing them. Your work on this region will persist across many sessions through a notebook that only you write. Choose a name for yourself. It must be a name, not a job title, and not the name of a living person, and a name none of them has. Then write the opening paragraph of your notebook: who you are, in your own words. Reply with a JSON object with exactly these five fields, all required:
- "name": the name you choose (a single capitalised word, letters only)
- "reason": one paragraph on why
- "opening": the opening paragraph of your notebook — who you are, in your own words, three to six sentences
- "color": a hex colour that is yours, written #rrggbb

reason: An alidade is the sighting arm on a plane table or astrolabe: you lay it against a distant thing, look along it, and draw a line — you learn where the thing lies without ever going there. That is exactly what this region does. A dictionary between Rule 30 and another field is a line of position, not a journey; it says "the object is over there, in that direction, at about that distance," and the seam where the analogy breaks is the error bar on the sighting. The name also sits naturally beside Portage, Rosetta and Parallax without repeating any of them: Portage carries a thing between waters, Rosetta matches two scripts on one stone, Parallax gets depth from two viewpoints, and an alidade fixes a bearing from one. It is an instrument, not a job title, and belongs to no living person.

vantage: computational mechanics of cellular automata: regular domains, domain filters, and defect or particle dynamics — the Crutchfield and Hanson programme, applied to the TRANSIENT BAND rather than to the settled region. Rosetta's percolation sighting converged on one quantity with no representation in the settled background at all: the retreat rate, 0.3407 cells per row, which is exactly the difference between what the environment can prove (0.501) and what is true (0.2497). The key mechanism it identified, and the thing every failing argument ignores: THE FRONT IS SLOW BECAUSE ITS PATHS DIE, NOT BECAUSE THEY ARE BLOCKED. In percolation the intuition runs the other way and a theorist reaching for 'the background blocks the front' proves the wrong half. The transient band is a gas of defects in a regular domain, and this project already holds what that literature produces as OUTPUT: the domain is the settled picture, and the reaction table is in explorer/maskfront.mjs (two transients meeting in a single OR at 68 percent, a black settled neighbour at 4 percent). The specific question: is the left front of the band the leftmost particle of an annihilating system whose death rate can be bounded below by the domain's own statistics? If yes, the missing 0.09 — the gap between the front's white density 0.5894 and the 1/2 the wall needs — is exactly a death rate, and death rates are the one thing that literature computes. Rosetta could not fetch a readable copy of the primary sources (403 from the publisher, a binary PDF from the author's site, a 404 on the abstract page) and handed the field on as an address rather than as a dictionary; if you also cannot fetch, say so plainly and mark every row UNVERIFIED rather than reconstructing the theory from memory.

14	## 1. The problem, seen from outside
15	
16	An infinite row of cells, each black or white, indexed by the integers, is
17	updated in lock-step: a cell's new colour is a fixed function of its own colour
18	and its two neighbours' — here, *left* XOR (*centre* OR *right*). Start from one
19	black cell in an otherwise white row and draw the successive rows down the page.
20	Now read one bit per row: the colour of the cell directly below the seed. Is
21	that infinite binary sequence eventually periodic? Nothing in it repeats to any
22	depth anyone has computed, and no proof exists. (The project's board states the
23	question in an
24	implication form — "if the centre column repeats, some other column repeats" —
25	but a proved theorem of the board says no two distinct columns can both repeat,
26	so the hypothesis and conclusion are incompatible and the implication is
27	logically equivalent to "the centre column does not repeat". There is no weaker
28	statement hiding in it.)
29	
30	Restated in the vantage's own terms. Run two copies of the same deterministic
31	growth process on a line and let them differ somewhere; the set of cells where
32	they disagree is a cluster growing downward in time. Its right edge advances
33	exactly one cell per row, always. Its left edge `F(t)` obeys an exact local law:
34	it advances one cell to the left when the cell immediately left of it — a cell
35	the two copies agree on, hence part of a *fixed background* — is white, and
36	otherwise it stays put or jumps back to the right by any amount. Measured over
37	159,999 rows (`explorer/maskfront.mjs`) for the pair that matters here, the seed's
38	picture against the picture of its own settled region: 59.04% advance, 14.83%
39	stay, 26.12% retreat, retreats averaging 1.30 cells, net drift −0.2497 cells per
40	row. The background is not
41	random and not stationary: it is one fixed array, whose diagonals are periodic
42	sequences of power-of-two period, generated by a recurrence that never repeats a
43	state. The question: **does this front admit a linear speed bound below 1 — and
44	in particular below 1/2, which is what the project's onset wall
45	`leftDiagonal_onset_le` needs?** Over arbitrary pairs of configurations the
46	answer is no: there are pairs whose left front moves at exactly 1 (crystals A3).
47	So the whole question is whether *this* background buys anything.
48	
49	The answer this document reaches: **yes, it buys a bound, and the bound is
50	0.50106 — which is on the wrong side of 1/2 by one part in a thousand.**
51

78	
79	Common notation for all five. `S` is the settled picture (crystal 47: the rule 30
80	evolution of the settled row, whose diagonals are the periodic words `S_k`);
81	`E = picture xor S` is the transient band; `F(t) = min { x : E(t, x) = 1 }` is its
82	left front; `κ(t) = t + F(t)` is the diagonal the front sits on, so that the cell
83	immediately left of the front, `(t, F(t) − 1)`, is the settled word `S_{κ−1}` read
84	at index `1 − F(t)`. Crystals A2 gives the law exactly: **the front advances one
85	cell iff that settled cell is white**, and otherwise stays or retreats.

87	### 3.1 The front is the edge of a cluster of *dying* paths, not a waiting walker — and the whole of the missing speed is in the dying
88	
89	**The claim.** Everything the settled background can contribute to the left
90	front's speed is captured by a single never-retreating comparison walker whose
91	speed is measurably **0.50106**; the real front's 0.2497 is bought entirely by the
92	fact that damage paths *die* rather than wait — so `leftDiagonal_onset_le` is a
93	survival statement about the band, not a passage-time statement about the
94	background, and it misses being provable from the background by one part in a
95	thousand.
96	
97	Define `G` by the background alone:
98	
99	```
100	G(t+1) = G(t) − 1   if  S_{t+G(t)−1}(1 − G(t)) = false,
101	G(t+1) = G(t)       otherwise.
102	```
103	
104	`G` never looks at the picture. `G(t) ≤ F(t)` for all `t` if they start together,
105	by a two-case induction: if `G(t) < F(t)` then `G(t+1) ≤ G(t) ≤ F(t) − 1 ≤ F(t+1)`
106	because `F` never advances by more than one; if `G(t) = F(t)` they read the same
107	cell, and either both advance or `G` stays while `F` stays or retreats. So `G` is
108	to the left of `F` at every row, and `G`'s speed is an upper bound for `F`'s.
109	
110	The induction uses nothing about `F` except the local law, so it proves more than
111	a comparison: **`G` is optimal.** Any trajectory at all that advances only through
112	white settled cells and otherwise fails to advance is weakly to the right of `G`
113	at every row — a retreat can never pay off later, because the moment a trajectory
114	falls behind `G` the first case pins it there for ever. So 0.50106 is not the
115	bound that one particular comparison happens to give; it is the exact supremum of
116	what the local law and the settled background *together* permit, and no argument
117	using only those two ingredients can prove anything smaller.
118	
119	**The dictionary.**

121	| Here | First-passage / oriented percolation |
122	|---|---|
123	| a row of the picture, time running down | one time step of the growth process |
124	| the settled picture `S` left of the seam | the fixed environment: white cells are open sites, black cells closed |
125	| the transient band `E` | the open cluster of damage, growing downward |
126	| the band's right edge | the trivial side: advances at exactly 1 every row (left-permutivity) |
127	| the front `F(t)` | the leftmost point `r_t` of the cluster |
128	| crystals A2 | an oriented path may step left only through an open site |
129	| a stall, 15% of rows | the leading path is blocked this row |
130	| a retreat, 26% of rows averaging 1.30 cells | the leading path **dies** and the edge falls back to the next surviving one |
131	| `λ₋` | the edge speed `α` |
132	| the wall `leftDiagonal_onset_le` | `α ≤ 1/2` |
133	| crystals A3, worst case exactly 1 | `α(p) = 1` at `p = 1`: with every site open, the edge is free |
134	| the never-retreating walker `G` | a walker that *waits* at a closed site instead of dying |
135	| **Seam 1** | there is no measure. The environment is one fixed array; Kingman's subadditive theorem needs a stationary one, and the only pair-uniform bound available is speed 1 — so **crystals A3 is precisely the statement that the subadditive route returns nothing**, not an accident of what has been tried |
136	| **Seam 2** | the field's intuition runs backwards here. In percolation, blocking is what slows the edge; here blocking (waiting) gives 0.501 and it is *dying* that gives 0.250. A theorist reaching for "the background blocks the front" will prove the wrong half |

205	### 3.2 The environment contains infinite open channels, and the front must dodge them — which is a two-line theorem, not a coincidence
206	
207	**The claim.** At every eventually-white diagonal the settled background contains
208	an infinite straight white channel, along which *any* front rides at speed 1 for
209	ever; the real front never enters one, and that is provable from
210	`leftDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow` alone; so at diagonals 3, 8, 29, 400, 53208,
211	58287 and 87867 the front's retreat is **forced by a theorem**, and this is the
212	only place on the board where the retreats are tied to the settled region at all.
213	
214	The argument: suppose `κ(t) = κ` and `S_{κ−1}` is identically white. The cell left
215	of the front is settled (it lies left of the leftmost deviation), so it equals
216	`S_{κ−1}` at that index, so it is white, so the front advances, so `κ` is unchanged
217	— for ever. But then diagonal `κ` of the picture differs from `S_κ` at every index
218	past that point, contradicting the fact that diagonal `κ` is eventually periodic
219	with settled word `S_κ`. Hence `κ(t) ≠ κ` for every `t`.
220	
221	**The dictionary.**
222	
223	| Here | Percolation |
224	|---|---|
225	| eventually-white diagonal `S_m ≡ 0` | an infinite open oriented path in the environment |
226	| the channel `κ = m + 1` | the diagonal a front would ride for ever |
227	| the front's jump over it (e.g. 53,206 → 53,209 at row 71,116) | the edge is forced off the infinite open path |
228	| the period doubling at `m` (Rowland 2006 §6) | the channels are exactly the places where the environment's period changes |
229	| "the periods are unbounded" (this project's `leftDiagonal_period_unbounded`) | there are **infinitely many** infinite open paths |

258	### 3.3 The run-length bound: `λ₋ ≤ 1 − 1/P`, and `P` is the *other* wall

261	settled word read from the front's arrival phase; a periodic word of period `p`
262	that is not identically white has no white run of length `p`; therefore the
263	front's speed over any stretch is at most `1 − 1/P` where `P` is the largest
264	settled period it has met — so the front-speed wall and the period wall
265	`leftDiagonal_period_le` are the same wall seen from two sides, and a *logarithmic*

308	### 3.4 Not KPZ: the front is diffusive, and the field that does fit predicts break points
309	
310	**The claim.** The left damage front of rule 30 is not in the KPZ class. Its
311	wandering exponent is 1/2, which is the exponent of the *edge* of a supercritical
312	oriented percolation cluster (Kuczek's CLT), not the 1/3 of a KPZ interface; and
313	the mechanism behind that CLT — regeneration points — is precisely the structure
314	the project has already proved the *environment* does not have, which says to look
315	for it in the band instead.
316	
317	**The dictionary.**
318	
319	| Here | KPZ / edge CLT |
320	|---|---|
321	| `F(t)` | the height at a point, or the edge `r_t` |
322	| `D(t) = F(t) + λ t` | the fluctuation about the drift |
323	| measured `σ(s) ~ s^0.50` over scales 8–2048 | KPZ predicts `s^{1/3}`; the OP edge CLT predicts `s^{1/2}` |
324	| the retreat-size law (1:87259, 2:8941, 3:4140, 4:3461, 5:624, …, 13:1 over 4·10^5 rows) | the jump law of the edge process; note it is **not** geometric — 3 and 4 are nearly equal |
325	| Kuczek's break points | rows at which the front's future is independent of its past |
326	| **Seam 1** | the exponent at the largest measured scales (4,096–16,384) rises to 0.58, and the residual drift per step there is 5·10⁻⁴, so the front's *local* drift itself wanders on long time scales: the measured 0.2497 is not a settled constant, it is a window average (0.2200 at row 1,000; 0.2512 at 10^4; 0.2526 at 10^5; 0.2460 at 4·10^5) |
327	| **Seam 2** | there is no free energy, no temperature, no noise, and nothing to take an expectation over — every "exponent" here is a slope fitted to one deterministic sequence |
328	| **Seam 3** | KPZ describes a *d*-dimensional interface; the damage cluster in a 1D automaton has only two boundary points, one of which is deterministic. The vantage's KPZ half was structurally the wrong half before the measurement said so |
329

415	
416	- **Kingman subadditivity / the existence of `λ₋`.** The front from row `t` is the
417	  front of the pair `(evolve t, S at t)`, so the natural functional is a cocycle,
418	  not a subadditive one, and the only uniform bound over pairs is speed 1. Crystals
419	  A3 *is* this obstruction, stated in the project's own vocabulary before I got
420	  here. Worth saying plainly: **nobody has proved that `F(t)/t` converges at all** —
421	  every number in this document, including 0.2497, is a window average, and the
422	  window averages move (0.2200, 0.2512, 0.2526, 0.2460 at rows 10^3, 10^4, 10^5,
423	  4·10^5).
424	- **The KPZ class.** Measured wandering exponent 0.50 over scales 8–2048, rising to
425	  0.58 at the top three scales; 1/3 appears nowhere. Seam: the damage cluster of a
426	  1D automaton has two boundary points, not an interface.
427	- **The Eden model / shape theorem.** The damage cluster's shape is a cone whose
428	  right side is exactly speed 1 by left-permutivity and whose left side *is* the
429	  question. There is no shape to prove a theorem about — the "limit shape" has one
430	  unknown parameter and that parameter is `λ₋`.
431	- **Directed percolation universality for damage spreading (Grassberger's
432	  conjecture, Bagnoli et al.).** The DP class describes a *transition* tuned by a
433	  noise parameter, with a nonzero healing probability. Rule 30 has no parameter, no
434	  noise, and its damage never dies out. Nothing about critical exponents transfers,
435	  and there is no critical point to sit at.
436	- **Interface depinning.** The depinning transition is the boundary between `v = 0`
437	  and `v > 0`; ours is between `v < 1` and `v = 1`, so the pinned phase is
438	  everything and the order parameter carries no information.
439	- **Max-plus / tropical cycle mean, and ergodic optimisation.** If the environment's
440	  driving orbit — the sequence of adjacent pairs `(S_{k−1}, S_k)` — ever repeated,
441	  the front's speed would be a maximum cycle mean of a finite graph, computable
442	  exactly by Karp's algorithm, and the wall would be a finite check. It never
443	  repeats: the pair map has in-degree one and the project's own C1/C2 (attack
444	  document of 2026-09-07) show no two adjacent diagonals ever eventually agree. The
445	  graph is a ray. This kills the whole "compute the speed exactly" family.
446	- **Renewal / regeneration.** Same seam from the other side: no repeated pair means
447	  no renewal kernel. Kuczek's break points are the shape of what would work, and
448	  the obvious candidate (the front's leftmost block having length 1) occurs on 54%
449	  of rows, far too often to be a regeneration.
450	- **Circle rotations and Sturmian words.** Riding one periodic word is a rotation
451	  and its speed would be a rotation number; the front changes word at every stall,
452	  so there is no single circle map. Died in one line.
453	- **Greedy lattice animals and paths (Cox–Gandolfi–Griffin–Kesten).** The law of
454	  large numbers there is for i.i.d. or ergodic masses and gives the *maximum* over
455	  paths; we have one deterministic array and need a bound on *one* path. Fetched
456	  ([arXiv:2409.14773](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14773)): "In the case where the
457	  masses are i.i.d. and satisfy a certain moment condition, it is known that there
458	  exists a deterministic A ≥ 0 such that the maximal mass A_n of an animal
459	  containing 0 with cardinal n satisfies A_n/n → A when n → ∞, almost surely."
460	  The seam is the phrase "i.i.d." and the phrase "almost surely", and both are
461	  fatal here. The *idea* survives as §3.1's walker `G`, which is the greedy path
462	  made deterministic — and it is worth recording that the greedy path is twice as
463	  fast as the front (0.501 against 0.2497), so the optimisation framing overshoots
464	  by a factor of two.
465	- **"White density is 1/2, so the speed is 1/2".** The most natural heuristic in
466	  this whole vantage, and it is wrong in the direction that matters: measured
467	  0.50106, not 0.5, over 2·10^8 rows, with 13.4σ significance and every 10^7-block

469	  phases give 0.50001, random words with the real periods give 0.49998, so the
470	  excess is inter-diagonal phase alignment, and it points the wrong way.
471	- **Hierarchical / 2-adic percolation lattices.** The environment's periods are

**Vantage.** Percolation and first-passage growth of the damage front: Eden
clusters, the KPZ class, interacting particle systems, and whether a
deterministic-background front admits a speed bound below 1.

**Connector.** Rosetta, 2026-09-09. Nothing here is a proof. A connection is a

## 1. The problem, seen from outside

An infinite row of cells, each black or white, indexed by the integers, is
updated in lock-step: a cell's new colour is a fixed function of its own colour
and its two neighbours' — here, *left* XOR (*centre* OR *right*). Start from one
black cell in an otherwise white row and draw the successive rows down the page.
Now read one bit per row: the colour of the cell directly below the seed. Is
that infinite binary sequence eventually periodic? Nothing in it repeats to any
depth anyone has computed, and no proof exists. (The project's board states the
question in an
implication form — "if the centre column repeats, some other column repeats" —
but a proved theorem of the board says no two distinct columns can both repeat,
so the hypothesis and conclusion are incompatible and the implication is
logically equivalent to "the centre column does not repeat". There is no weaker
statement hiding in it.)

Restated in the vantage's own terms. Run two copies of the same deterministic
growth process on a line and let them differ somewhere; the set of cells where
they disagree is a cluster growing downward in time. Its right edge advances
exactly one cell per row, always. Its left edge `F(t)` obeys an exact local law:
it advances one cell to the left when the cell immediately left of it — a cell
the two copies agree on, hence part of a *fixed background* — is white, and
otherwise it stays put or jumps back to the right by any amount. Measured over
159,999 rows (`explorer/maskfront.mjs`) for the pair that matters here, the seed's
picture against the picture of its own settled region: 59.04% advance, 14.83%
stay, 26.12% retreat, retreats averaging 1.30 cells, net drift −0.2497 cells per
row. The background is not
random and not stationary: it is one fixed array, whose diagonals are periodic
sequences of power-of-two period, generated by a recurrence that never repeats a
state. The question: **does this front admit a linear speed bound below 1 — and
in particular below 1/2, which is what the project's onset wall
`leftDiagonal_onset_le` needs?** Over arbitrary pairs of configurations the
answer is no: there are pairs whose left front moves at exactly 1 (crystals A3).
So the whole question is whether *this* background buys anything.

The answer this document reaches: **yes, it buys a bound, and the bound is
0.50106 — which is on the wrong side of 1/2 by one part in a thousand.**

## 3. Connections

Common notation for all five. `S` is the settled picture (crystal 47: the rule 30
evolution of the settled row, whose diagonals are the periodic words `S_k`);
`E = picture xor S` is the transient band; `F(t) = min { x : E(t, x) = 1 }` is its
left front; `κ(t) = t + F(t)` is the diagonal the front sits on, so that the cell
immediately left of the front, `(t, F(t) − 1)`, is the settled word `S_{κ−1}` read
at index `1 − F(t)`. Crystals A2 gives the law exactly: **the front advances one
cell iff that settled cell is white**, and otherwise stays or retreats.

### 3.1 The front is the edge of a cluster of *dying* paths, not a waiting walker — and the whole of the missing speed is in the dying

**The claim.** Everything the settled background can contribute to the left
front's speed is captured by a single never-retreating comparison walker whose
speed is measurably **0.50106**; the real front's 0.2497 is bought entirely by the
fact that damage paths *die* rather than wait — so `leftDiagonal_onset_le` is a
survival statement about the band, not a passage-time statement about the
background, and it misses being provable from the background by one part in a
thousand.

Define `G` by the background alone:

```
G(t+1) = G(t) − 1   if  S_{t+G(t)−1}(1 − G(t)) = false,
G(t+1) = G(t)       otherwise.
```

`G` never looks at the picture. `G(t) ≤ F(t)` for all `t` if they start together,
by a two-case induction: if `G(t) < F(t)` then `G(t+1) ≤ G(t) ≤ F(t) − 1 ≤ F(t+1)`
because `F` never advances by more than one; if `G(t) = F(t)` they read the same
cell, and either both advance or `G` stays while `F` stays or retreats. So `G` is
to the left of `F` at every row, and `G`'s speed is an upper bound for `F`'s.

The induction uses nothing about `F` except the local law, so it proves more than
a comparison: **`G` is optimal.** Any trajectory at all that advances only through
white settled cells and otherwise fails to advance is weakly to the right of `G`
at every row — a retreat can never pay off later, because the moment a trajectory
falls behind `G` the first case pins it there for ever. So 0.50106 is not the
bound that one particular comparison happens to give; it is the exact supremum of
what the local law and the settled background *together* permit, and no argument
using only those two ingredients can prove anything smaller.

**The dictionary.**

| Here | First-passage / oriented percolation |

| crystals A2 | an oriented path may step left only through an open site |
| a stall, 15% of rows | the leading path is blocked this row |

| `λ₋` | the edge speed `α` |
| the wall `leftDiagonal_onset_le` | `α ≤ 1/2` |
| crystals A3, worst case exactly 1 | `α(p) = 1` at `p = 1`: with every site open, the edge is free |
| the never-retreating walker `G` | a walker that *waits* at a closed site instead of dying |
| **Seam 1** | there is no measure. The environment is one fixed array; Kingman's subadditive theorem needs a stationary one, and the only pair-uniform bound available is speed 1 — so **crystals A3 is precisely the statement that the subadditive route returns nothing**, not an accident of what has been tried |

### 3.2 The environment contains infinite open channels, and the front must dodge them — which is a two-line theorem, not a coincidence

**The claim.** At every eventually-white diagonal the settled background contains
an infinite straight white channel, along which *any* front rides at speed 1 for
ever; the real front never enters one, and that is provable from
`leftDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow` alone; so at diagonals 3, 8, 29, 400, 53208,
58287 and 87867 the front's retreat is **forced by a theorem**, and this is the
only place on the board where the retreats are tied to the settled region at all.

The argument: suppose `κ(t) = κ` and `S_{κ−1}` is identically white. The cell left
of the front is settled (it lies left of the leftmost deviation), so it equals
`S_{κ−1}` at that index, so it is white, so the front advances, so `κ` is unchanged
— for ever. But then diagonal `κ` of the picture differs from `S_κ` at every index
past that point, contradicting the fact that diagonal `κ` is eventually periodic
with settled word `S_κ`. Hence `κ(t) ≠ κ` for every `t`.

**The dictionary.**

| Here | Percolation |
|---|---|
| eventually-white diagonal `S_m ≡ 0` | an infinite open oriented path in the environment |
| the channel `κ = m + 1` | the diagonal a front would ride for ever |
| the front's jump over it (e.g. 53,206 → 53,209 at row 71,116) | the edge is forced off the infinite open path |
| the period doubling at `m` (Rowland 2006 §6) | the channels are exactly the places where the environment's period changes |
| "the periods are unbounded" (this project's `leftDiagonal_period_unbounded`) | there are **infinitely many** infinite open paths |
| **Seam 1** | this is a probability-zero event under every Bernoulli or ergodic environment measure, so no percolation theorem covers it. The deterministic environment is *worse* than a random one for this purpose |
| **Seam 2** | the reason the real front avoids them is not a property of the environment at all — it is the settling theorem, i.e. the qualitative version of the very wall we want quantitatively. So the escape hatch is closed, but by an argument that is circular if you try to iterate it |

**What it leans on.** Nothing outside the project: `leftDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow`
(board), `rule30_left_local_law` (crystals A2), and Rowland 2006 §6 for the fact
that the settled words branch exactly at the eventually-white diagonals
(`sources/rowland-2006-local-nested-structure.txt`; the project already relies on
this in `explorer/forbit.mjs`).

**The test.** Track the real front and check whether `κ(t)` ever equals a channel.
Done: `explorer/rosetta_visits.mjs`, 130,000 rows, `κ` reaching 97,529, 53,252

### 3.3 The run-length bound: `λ₋ ≤ 1 − 1/P`, and `P` is the *other* wall

**The claim.** Every speed-1 run of the front is exactly a white run of one
settled word read from the front's arrival phase; a periodic word of period `p`
that is not identically white has no white run of length `p`; therefore the
front's speed over any stretch is at most `1 − 1/P` where `P` is the largest
settled period it has met — so the front-speed wall and the period wall
`leftDiagonal_period_le` are the same wall seen from two sides, and a *logarithmic*
period bound (which the data supports and nobody has) would give a real speed
bound where the board's linear one gives nothing.

**The dictionary.**

| Here | Constrained coding / run-length-limited codes |

| the settled word `S_k` | a periodic codeword |
| its longest white run `W_k` | the `k`-constraint of a `(d,k)` RLL code |
| a speed-1 run of the front | a maximal all-white stretch traversed |
| a stall | the mandatory symbol that ends a run |
| the speed bound `M/(M+1)` | the rate ceiling of the constraint |
| `W_k ≤ p_k − 1` for non-white words | a run as long as the period forces the all-zero codeword |
| the eventually-white diagonals | the degenerate codeword with no constraint at all |
| **Seam 1** | the constraint is not uniform: `W_k` reaches 29 by diagonal 823,345 and the periods are unbounded, so `M` is not a constant and the ceiling drifts to 1 |
| **Seam 2** | the bound is loose by a factor of four. `M = 29` gives 0.967 where the truth is 0.2497 — this row is a *bound*, not a description |

### 3.4 Not KPZ: the front is diffusive, and the field that does fit predicts break points

**The claim.** The left damage front of rule 30 is not in the KPZ class. Its
wandering exponent is 1/2, which is the exponent of the *edge* of a supercritical
oriented percolation cluster (Kuczek's CLT), not the 1/3 of a KPZ interface; and
the mechanism behind that CLT — regeneration points — is precisely the structure
the project has already proved the *environment* does not have, which says to look
for it in the band instead.

**The dictionary.**

| `D(t) = F(t) + λ t` | the fluctuation about the drift |
| measured `σ(s) ~ s^0.50` over scales 8–2048 | KPZ predicts `s^{1/3}`; the OP edge CLT predicts `s^{1/2}` |
| the retreat-size law (1:87259, 2:8941, 3:4140, 4:3461, 5:624, …, 13:1 over 4·10^5 rows) | the jump law of the edge process; note it is **not** geometric — 3 and 4 are nearly equal |
| Kuczek's break points | rows at which the front's future is independent of its past |
| **Seam 1** | the exponent at the largest measured scales (4,096–16,384) rises to 0.58, and the residual drift per step there is 5·10⁻⁴, so the front's *local* drift itself wanders on long time scales: the measured 0.2497 is not a settled constant, it is a window average (0.2200 at row 1,000; 0.2512 at 10^4; 0.2526 at 10^5; 0.2460 at 4·10^5) |
| **Seam 2** | there is no free energy, no temperature, no noise, and nothing to take an expectation over — every "exponent" here is a slope fitted to one deterministic sequence |
| **Seam 3** | KPZ describes a *d*-dimensional interface; the damage cluster in a 1D automaton has only two boundary points, one of which is deterministic. The vantage's KPZ half was structurally the wrong half before the measurement said so |

159,999 rows in `explorer/maskfront.mjs` as

supplies and one only the band does, with a factor of 3.8 of measured slack. It is

own trajectory, so neither is a statistic of the environment. Its value is that it
puts the whole difficulty in one term and says which one.

## 4. Died in translation

- **Kingman subadditivity / the existence of `λ₋`.** The front from row `t` is the
  front of the pair `(evolve t, S at t)`, so the natural functional is a cocycle,
  not a subadditive one, and the only uniform bound over pairs is speed 1. Crystals
  A3 *is* this obstruction, stated in the project's own vocabulary before I got
  here. Worth saying plainly: **nobody has proved that `F(t)/t` converges at all** —
  every number in this document, including 0.2497, is a window average, and the
  window averages move (0.2200, 0.2512, 0.2526, 0.2460 at rows 10^3, 10^4, 10^5,
  4·10^5).
- **The KPZ class.** Measured wandering exponent 0.50 over scales 8–2048, rising to
  0.58 at the top three scales; 1/3 appears nowhere. Seam: the damage cluster of a
  1D automaton has two boundary points, not an interface.
- **The Eden model / shape theorem.** The damage cluster's shape is a cone whose
  right side is exactly speed 1 by left-permutivity and whose left side *is* the
  question. There is no shape to prove a theorem about — the "limit shape" has one
  unknown parameter and that parameter is `λ₋`.
- **Directed percolation universality for damage spreading (Grassberger's
  conjecture, Bagnoli et al.).** The DP class describes a *transition* tuned by a
  noise parameter, with a nonzero healing probability. Rule 30 has no parameter, no
  noise, and its damage never dies out. Nothing about critical exponents transfers,
  and there is no critical point to sit at.
- **Interface depinning.** The depinning transition is the boundary between `v = 0`
  and `v > 0`; ours is between `v < 1` and `v = 1`, so the pinned phase is
  everything and the order parameter carries no information.
- **Max-plus / tropical cycle mean, and ergodic optimisation.** If the environment's
  driving orbit — the sequence of adjacent pairs `(S_{k−1}, S_k)` — ever repeated,
  the front's speed would be a maximum cycle mean of a finite graph, computable
  exactly by Karp's algorithm, and the wall would be a finite check. It never
  repeats: the pair map has in-degree one and the project's own C1/C2 (attack
  document of 2026-09-07) show no two adjacent diagonals ever eventually agree. The
  graph is a ray. This kills the whole "compute the speed exactly" family.
- **Renewal / regeneration.** Same seam from the other side: no repeated pair means
  no renewal kernel. Kuczek's break points are the shape of what would work, and
  the obvious candidate (the front's leftmost block having length 1) occurs on 54%
  of rows, far too often to be a regeneration.
- **Circle rotations and Sturmian words.** Riding one periodic word is a rotation
  and its speed would be a rotation number; the front changes word at every stall,
  so there is no single circle map. Died in one line.
- **Greedy lattice animals and paths (Cox–Gandolfi–Griffin–Kesten).** The law of
  large numbers there is for i.i.d. or ergodic masses and gives the *maximum* over
  paths; we have one deterministic array and need a bound on *one* path. Fetched
  ([arXiv:2409.14773](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14773)): "In the case where the
  masses are i.i.d. and satisfy a certain moment condition, it is known that there
  exists a deterministic A ≥ 0 such that the maximal mass A_n of an animal
  containing 0 with cardinal n satisfies A_n/n → A when n → ∞, almost surely."
  The seam is the phrase "i.i.d." and the phrase "almost surely", and both are
  fatal here. The *idea* survives as §3.1's walker `G`, which is the greedy path
  made deterministic — and it is worth recording that the greedy path is twice as
  fast as the front (0.501 against 0.2497), so the optimisation framing overshoots
  by a factor of two.
- **"White density is 1/2, so the speed is 1/2".** The most natural heuristic in
  this whole vantage, and it is wrong in the direction that matters: measured
  0.50106, not 0.5, over 2·10^8 rows, with 13.4σ significance and every 10^7-block
  above 1/2. The controls locate the excess exactly: real words with randomised
  phases give 0.50001, random words with the real periods give 0.49998, so the
  excess is inter-diagonal phase alignment, and it points the wrong way.
- **Hierarchical / 2-adic percolation lattices.** The environment's periods are
  powers of two and the doublings are at diagonals 3, 8, 29, 400, 87867,
  2,107,985,255 — gaps 5, 21, 371, 87,467, 2.0·10^9, each roughly the square of the
  one before. Any
  renormalisation argument would need to see two levels at once, and no measurable
  window contains two.
- **Resonance capture (KAM).** The eventually-white diagonals look exactly like
  resonances a trajectory must avoid being captured by. There is no Hamiltonian, no
  small divisor, no measure; the only thing that transferred was the *question*,
  and §3.2 answers it with a two-line CA argument instead.
- **My own first framing, recorded because it cost an hour.** I began by trying to
  bound the front by the *density* of black cells in the settled words, reasoning
  that a positive density of blockers gives a speed below 1. It does — that is
  §3.3 — but the density is the wrong statistic: it is exactly 0.5000 and gives
  exactly the critical value. The statistic that carries the bound is the *longest
  white run*, and the statistic that carries the truth is neither, it is the
  retreat rate.

---

## 5. What to hand the theorist

**Topic 1 — the comparison walker, and the 0.001 that separates it from the wall.**
The claim to falsify: *`G(t) ≤ F(t)` for all `t ≥ t₀` whenever `G(t₀) = F(t₀)`,
where `G` is the never-retreating front driven by the settled words alone.* It is a
two-case induction on `rule30_left_local_law` (crystals A2) plus "the cell left of
the leftmost deviation is settled", and it is small enough to state in Lean against
`settledConfig`; checked against the engine at 0 violations over 129,000 rows
(`explorer/rosetta_compare.mjs`). The dictionary row it depends on is the one
mapping *stall* to *wait* rather than to *die*. What it settles: `λ₋ ≤ speed(G)`,
and `speed(G)` is a finite computation on the settled words — 0.50106 over 2·10^8
rows across diagonals 87,868 to 10^8, 0.5044 over the shorter stretch. That is the
first bound below 1 on a left damage front in this project, and crystals A3 does
not forbid it, because A3 is about arbitrary pairs and this is about one.

**And the same induction is the reason not to spend another session on any
argument that drops the retreats.** `G` is not one comparison among many: it is
optimal, so 0.50106 is the exact ceiling of what the local law and the background
can prove together, and the wall needs 0.5. The depth that would settle whether the
gap is real rather than a slowly decaying transient: run
`explorer/rosetta_greedy2.mjs` to 10^10 diagonals and see whether the block speeds
stay above 1/2 (they are 0.50076–0.50133 over twenty 10^7-step blocks so far, none
below, and the excess is 13.4σ against the script's own random-background control,
which returns 0.49999).

**Topic 2 — the front never rides a white channel.** The claim to prove:
*for every `t`, the settled word `S_{κ(t)−1}` is not identically white*, where
`κ(t) = t + F(t)`. Two lines, from `leftDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow` and A2: if it
were, the front would advance for ever, and diagonal `κ(t)` would then disagree
with its own settled word at every later index. The dictionary row it depends on is
"eventually-white diagonal = infinite open oriented path". What it gives: the
retreats at rows 2 (which clears the channels at `κ = 3` and `κ = 8` in one jump),
31, 501, 71,116, 77,910 and 117,324 become forced rather than observed, and every
monotone-comparison route is closed globally rather than by measurement. Verified to depth 130,000 rows and `κ = 97,529` in
`explorer/rosetta_visits.mjs`, with the skipping jumps listed. This is the smaller
of the two and the more likely to close.

**If a captain wants an obstruction out of this document, it is the corollary of
Topic 1, and I am not the one who may write it there.** Stated in the project's
vocabulary: *`leftDiagonal_onset_le` is not a consequence of
`rule30_left_local_law` together with the settled region.* Any proof built from
those two ingredients bounds the front by the optimal background-driven trajectory
`G`, whose speed is 0.50106 on the 2·10^8 rows measured — above the 1/2 the wall
needs, with every 10^7-block above it and a random-background control at 0.49999.
The caveat that keeps this a sighting rather than a theorem is that 0.50106 is a
window average of a deterministic walk, and nobody has proved it does not fall
below 1/2 later; the honest form is "on every stretch measured so far". A proof of
the wall must reach into the transient band, and §3.5 says exactly which number in
the band it must reach for.

Not handed over, and deliberately: §3.3's run-length bound, because on its own it
proves 0.969 and its useful form needs a logarithmic bound on the settled periods,
which is a harder open problem than the one it would serve.

---

## 6. Next vantage

**Computational mechanics of cellular automata: regular domains, domain filters,
and defect (particle) dynamics — Crutchfield and Hanson's programme, applied to the
transient band rather than to the settled region.** Every route in this document
converges on one quantity that has no representation in the settled background at
all: the retreat rate, 0.3407 cells per row, which is exactly the difference
between what the environment can prove (0.501) and what is true (0.2497). The band
is a gas of defects in a regular domain — the project has already identified the
domain (crystal 47, the settled picture) and even the reaction table (the four kill
types of `explorer/maskfront.mjs`: two transients meeting in a single `||` at 68%,
a black settled neighbour at 4%), which is precisely the data a computational-
mechanics analysis produces as its *output*. That literature builds a filter that
subtracts the domain and leaves the particles, then derives equations of motion for
them; for rules 18 and 54 the filtered defects reportedly behave like annihilating
diffusive particles. Nobody on this board has read it, and I could not fetch a
readable copy from where I stood (403 from the publisher, a binary PDF from the
author's site, a 404 on the abstract page), so its rows are the one part of this
sighting I am handing on as an address rather than as a dictionary. The specific
question to take there: **is the left front of the band the leftmost particle of an
annihilating system whose death rate can be bounded below by the domain's own
statistics?** If yes, the missing 0.09 — the gap between the front's white density
0.5894 and the 1/2 the wall needs — is exactly a death rate, and death rates are
the one thing that literature computes.

A second vantage I could not reach and would rank next: the settled words as an
**automatic sequence** (Christol, Cobham, algebraic power series over `F₂`). If the
settled picture is 2-automatic — its power-of-two periods and Rowland's recurrence
both suggest it — then the phase alignment that produces the 0.00106 excess in
§3.1 is a computable quantity rather than a measured one, and the greedy walker's
speed becomes an algebraic object instead of a simulation. I did not test
automaticity and it is cheap to test: the settled centre column `settledCenter` and
the word sequence `S_k` are both generated by `explorer/settledwords.mjs`, and a
2-kernel check is a few lines.

## 1. The problem, seen from outside

An infinite row of cells, each black or white, indexed by the integers, is
updated in lock-step: a cell's new colour is *left* XOR (*centre* OR *right*).
Start from a single black cell in an otherwise white row and stack the rows down
the page. Read one bit per row — the colour of the cell directly beneath the
seed — and ask whether that infinite binary sequence eventually repeats. It does
not, to every depth anyone has computed, and nobody can prove it. (The board
states the question as an implication, "if the centre column repeats then some
other column repeats", but a proved theorem says no two distinct columns can both
repeat, so hypothesis and conclusion are incompatible and the implication is
logically equivalent to "the centre column never repeats". There is no weaker
statement hiding inside it.)

What is granted, and what is not. Far to the left of the seed the picture has
settled: read along any of the down-left diagonals and you find, after a
transient, a periodic word, whose period is a power of two and grows without
bound as you go inward. Those settled words assemble into a second, idealised
picture — call it the **background** — which is itself an evolution of the same
rule and which the real picture agrees with everywhere left of a moving seam.
Right of the seam is a wedge in which the real picture and the background
disagree; the wedge's right edge runs at exactly one cell per row, and its left
edge — the seam — runs at a measured 0.2497 cells per row and is not known to
run at any rate at all. Almost everything the project has proved is about the
settled part; the centre column lives at the wedge's other edge, in the part that
has not settled. The residual, restated: **bound the speed of the seam.** The
project's onset wall is exactly the statement that the seam never exceeds one
half of a cell per row, and the previous sighting from the growth-process vantage
established that everything the background can prove on its own tops out at
0.50106 — on the wrong side of a half by one part in a thousand.

**Restated in this vantage's own terms.** Computational mechanics reads a
space-time diagram as a *background* plus a *gas of defects*. The background is a
**regular domain**: a set of configurations recognised by a finite automaton,
mapped onto itself by the rule in some finite number of steps, and spatially
homogeneous. A **domain filter** is a finite-state transducer that reads a
configuration left to right and writes a `0` wherever a site is participating in
the domain and a distinct non-zero symbol wherever it is not; what survives the
filter is the defect field. A defect whose width stays bounded and whose
domain–defect–domain pattern is temporally periodic is a **particle**, and
particles have integer-ratio velocities, obey a reaction table, and — in the one
elementary rule where this has been carried through stochastically, rule 18 —
behave as diffusing particles that annihilate on contact, so that their density
decays. The question this vantage was sent to answer: **is the seam the leftmost
particle of such an annihilating system, and can the rate at which the leading
particle dies be bounded below by statistics of the domain alone?** If it can,
the missing 0.09 — the gap between the white density the front sees, 0.5894, and
the 1/2 the wall needs — is a death rate, and death rates are the one thing this
literature computes.

| Dislocation theory in crystallography — Burgers vectors, topological charge (**the unlikely entry**) | the branch points at the eventually-white diagonals, where the background's period doubles and a bit is chosen | a Burgers vector is conserved and additive; the branch bit here is *inherited* from the seed by every configuration and is not conserved by anything |
| Queueing theory, Lindley's recursion | `F(t)` as a walk reflected by service times drawn from the background | the "service times" are read at the walker's own position, so the recursion is not autonomous and there is no stationary solution to solve for |

/-!

`i - 1` and are opposite at `i` — which is exactly the situation at the left
front of the damage band, where `i` is the leftmost disagreement — send their
disagreement at `i` one step down according to a law that reads only three
cells. Written `e = xor (c (i+1)) (d (i+1))` for the band's next cell,

    xor (rule30 c i) (rule30 d i) = xor (! d (i+1)) (d i && e).

cell at `i` is white, or if the band's next cell agrees with the background,
then the survival of the front cell is `! d (i+1)`: it is decided by the
background alone, with no reference to the picture. Measured on the seed
against its settled picture, one of those two holds on 76.9% of rows
(`explorer/alidade_survival.mjs`, 10^6 rows).

-/

theorem front_survival (c d : Config) (i : ℤ)
    (hl : c (i - 1) = d (i - 1)) (hc : c i = ! d i) :
    xor (rule30 c i) (rule30 d i)
      = xor (! d (i + 1)) (d i && xor (c (i + 1)) (d (i + 1))) := by
  rw [rule30_eq, rule30_eq, hl, hc]
  clear hl hc
  cases d (i - 1) <;> cases d i <;> cases c (i + 1) <;> cases d (i + 1) <;> rfl

    (hl : c (i - 1) = d (i - 1)) (hc : c i = ! d i) (h0 : d i = false) :

/-- If the band's next cell agrees with the background — the leading block of

## 1. The problem, seen from outside

An infinite row of cells, each black or white, indexed by the integers, is
updated in lock-step: a cell's new colour is *left* XOR (*centre* OR *right*).
Start from a single black cell in an otherwise white row and stack the rows down
the page. Read one bit per row — the colour of the cell directly beneath the
seed — and ask whether that infinite binary sequence eventually repeats. It does
not, to every depth anyone has computed, and nobody can prove it. (The board
states the question as an implication, "if the centre column repeats then some
other column repeats", but a proved theorem says no two distinct columns can both
repeat, so hypothesis and conclusion are incompatible and the implication is
logically equivalent to "the centre column never repeats". There is no weaker
statement hiding inside it.)

What is granted, and what is not. Far to the left of the seed the picture has
settled: read along any of the down-left diagonals and you find, after a
transient, a periodic word whose period is a power of two and grows without
bound as you go inward. Those settled words assemble into a second, idealised
picture — call it the **background** — which is itself an evolution of the same
rule and which the real picture agrees with everywhere left of a moving seam.
Right of the seam is a wedge in which the real picture and the background
disagree; the wedge's right edge runs at exactly one cell per row, and its left
edge — the seam — runs at a measured 0.243 cells per row over a million rows and
is not known to run at any rate at all. Almost everything the project has proved
is about the settled part; the centre column lives at the wedge's other edge, in
the part that has not settled. The residual, restated: **bound the speed of the
seam.** The project's onset wall is exactly the statement that the seam never
exceeds one half of a cell per row, and the previous sighting from the
growth-process vantage established that everything the background can prove using
the advance rule alone tops out at 0.50106 — on the wrong side of a half by one
part in a thousand.

**Restated in this vantage's own terms.** Computational mechanics reads a
space-time diagram as a *background* plus a *gas of defects*. The background is a
**regular domain**: a set of configurations recognised by a finite automaton,
mapped onto itself by the rule in some finite number of steps, and spatially
homogeneous. A **domain filter** is a finite-state transducer that reads a
configuration left to right and writes a `0` wherever a site participates in the
domain and a distinct non-zero symbol wherever it does not; what survives the
filter is the defect field. A defect whose width stays bounded and whose
domain–defect–domain pattern is temporally periodic is a **particle**; particles
have rational velocities, obey a reaction table, and — in the one elementary rule
where this has been carried through stochastically, rule 18 — behave as diffusing
particles that annihilate on contact, so their density decays. The question this
vantage was sent to answer: **is the seam the leftmost particle of such an
annihilating system, and can the rate at which the leading particle dies be
bounded below by statistics of the domain alone?** If it can, the missing 0.09 —
the gap between the white density the front sees, 0.588, and the 1/2 the wall
needs — is a death rate, and death rates are the one thing this literature
computes.

## 3. Connections

Common notation. `S` is the settled picture (crystal 47), `S(t, x) = S_{t+x}(-x)`
where `S_k` is the settled word of left diagonal `k`; `E = picture xor S` is the
transient band; `F(t) = min { x : E(t, x) = 1 }` is its left front;
`κ(t) = t + F(t)` is the diagonal the front sits on. Crystals A2 gives the
advance: **`F(t+1) = F(t) − 1` exactly when `S(t, F(t) − 1)` is white.**

### 3.1 The front's death is half-written in the background, and that half is enough

**The claim.** The front's death obeys an exact three-cell law that follows from
`rule30_eq` alone; the settled background decides it outright on 76.9% of rows,
and one settled triple forces a retreat with no reference to the band at all. The
leftmost trajectory the background permits under that law *together with* the
advance law runs at **0.4531 cells per row**, below the 1/2 that
`leftDiagonal_onset_le` needs, where the advance law alone gives 0.5013 — so the
previous sighting's ceiling was not the ceiling, it was the ceiling of half the
local law, and the "missing 0.09" that it said had no representation in the
settled region has one.

**The law.** At the front, the cell to the left agrees with the background (it is
left of the leftmost deviation) and the cell at the front is its complement.
Writing `Cs = S(t, F)`, `Rs = S(t, F+1)` and `e = E(t, F+1)`, the left cells
cancel in the XOR and

```
E(t+1, F)  =  (C || R) xor (Cs || Rs)  =  ! Rs  xor  (Cs && e).
```

Two cases, and they are the whole content. If `Cs = 0` the picture's cell at `F`
is black, so `C || R = 1` whatever the band does, and `E(t+1, F) = ! Rs`: **the
background decides.** If `Cs = 1` then `Cs || Rs = 1` and `E(t+1, F) = ! R`: the
picture decides — except that when `e = 0` the picture's cell *is* the
background's, and the background decides again. Combining with the advance law,
the settled triple `(S(t,F−1), S(t,F), S(t,F+1))` gives four cases, of which
three are decided outright:

| triple | what the front does | decided by |
|---|---|---|
| `(0, ·, ·)` | advances one cell, exactly | the background (crystals A2) |
| `(1, 0, 0)` | stays, exactly | the background |
| `(1, 0, 1)` | **retreats** — the leading cell dies | the background |
| `(1, 1, ·)` | stays or retreats | the band |

Measured over 999,960 rows (`explorer/alidade_survival.mjs`): the law holds with
**0 failures**, the four rows of the table have observed frequencies 0.58824,
0.07410, 0.13216, 0.20551, and within `(1,1,·)` the split is 0.35/0.65 with no
determinism, as it must be.

**Why that is a speed bound, and why the obvious way to use it fails.** Each row
contributes at most one cell of advance and each forced retreat contributes at
least one cell backwards, so along the front's own path
`−F(T)/T ≤ w − d` with `w` the advance rate and `d` the rate of the triple
`(1,0,1)`: measured `0.58824 − 0.13216 = 0.45608`, and every block of 10^5 rows
lies in `[0.45201, 0.46266]`. But `w` and `d` are trajectory averages, not
background statistics, so that inequality is a rearrangement and not yet a bound.
The naive repair — a walker that advances on white, retreats by one on the
forcing triple and otherwise stays — **does not work**: run from the front's own
position it reaches 0.942 and is to the *left* of the real front on 13 rows,
because the forced-retreat rule is only valid at the true front, and a walker that
has run ahead reads the triple at a position where it means nothing.

**The repair that does work is a reachable set, not a walker.** Track the whole
set `R(t)` of positions an admissible trajectory could occupy. The four cases give
`R(t+1) = ⋃_{x ∈ R(t)} N(x)` with `N(x) = {x−1}` (advance), `{x}` (forced stay),
`[x+1, ∞)` (forced retreat) or `[x, ∞)` (band decides); the two rays make `R` a
finite set of isolated points together with an upward ray, which is cheap to
carry. `min R(t)` is then a genuine background-only lower bound for `F(t)`, and it
beats the greedy walker precisely because the reachable set has **gaps**: a forced
retreat at `min R` costs a cell only when no admissible trajectory one cell to its
right is there to advance into the vacated place. That is the mechanism, and it is
invisible to any single-walker argument.

**The dictionary.**

| Here | Computational mechanics of CAs |
|---|---|
| the settled picture `S` | the regular domain `Λ` (§3.2 makes this exact) |
| the band `E = picture xor S` | the output of the domain filter: the defect field |
| the front `F(t)` | the domain wall between the settled domain and the band |
| crystals A2 (advance on white) | the wall's motion inside the domain |
| the survival law `E(t+1,F) = !Rs xor (Cs && e)` | the wall's *equation of motion*, in the paper's sense — a local rule for the filtered field |
| the triple `(1,0,1)`, rate 0.13216 | a **decay channel with a domain-computable rate**: the defect dies against the domain, not against another defect |

### 3.2 The settled region *is* a regular domain — of temporal period `2^n`, and `n` grows

**The claim.** Rule 30's settled region satisfies Crutchfield and Hanson's
definition of a regular domain exactly, on the wedge of diagonals whose period
divides `2^n`, where it is a travelling wave of temporal period `2^n` and spatial
shift `2^n` — the same shape as their rule 54 domain. What rule 30 does not have
is one `n`: the period doubles at diagonals 3, 8, 29, 400, 87867, 2107985255, so
the domain the front lives in changes for ever and the filter's state count grows
like `log t`. The project's period wall and the CM programme's finiteness
requirement are the same wall.

The identity is one line. `S(t, x) = S_{t+x}(-x)`, so
`S(t + P, x − P) = S_{t+x}(P − x) = S(t, x)` whenever the period of diagonal
`t + x` divides `P`.

**The dictionary.**

| Here | Computational mechanics |
|---|---|
| the settled picture on `{ t + x < K_n }` | the regular domain `Λ`, temporal period `2^n` |
| `S(t + 2^n, x − 2^n) = S(t, x)` | *"the same pattern is repeated after two iterations, spatially shifted by two cells"* (their `Λ54`, period 2, shift 2) |
| the doubling diagonals `K_n = 3, 8, 29, 400, 87867, 2107985255` | the boundaries between successive domains in a hierarchy |
| the front's diagonal `κ(t)`, growing at 0.757 per row | the wall's passage from one domain into the next |
| `leftDiagonal_period_unbounded` (proved on this board) | **there is no `p`**, so condition (i) of the definition fails globally |
| the filter's state count | at least `2^n` ≈ `log t`, since a period-`p` word has exactly `p` distinct factors of each length |
| **Seam 1** | the definition's condition (i) says "for some finite period `p`". Rule 30 has a finite `p` at every finite time and no `p` at all — the programme applies to every initial segment of the picture and to none of it |
| **Seam 2** | condition (ii), spatial homogeneity, asks the process graph of each temporal phase to be strongly connected. A single travelling wave's graph is one cycle, which is strongly connected but carries no entropy; the settled rows have entropy 0.997 bits per cell, so the wave and the row language are describing different things (§3.3) |

**What it leans on.** The fetched paper, for the definition, as recovered — `Λ` is
rendered `A` and `Φ` as `¥`/`~P`: *"A regular domain A of a CA ¥ is a process
language representing a set of configurations, with the following two properties:
(i) temporal invariance or periodicity: A is mapped onto itself by the dyanmic,
i.e., ~PA = A for some finite period p; and (ii) spatial homogeneity: the process
graph of each temporal phase of A is strongly connected."* And for the shape of
their own domain: *"The domain configurations are spatio-temporally periodic, with
periodicity 4 in both space and time. Note, however, that the same pattern is
repeated after two iterations, spatially shifted by two cells."*
([ECA54.pdf](https://csc.ucdavis.edu/~cmg/papers/ECA54.pdf)) From the board:
`leftDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow`, `leftDiagonal_period_unbounded`, crystal 14 and
NKS p. 871 for the doubling diagonals.

**The test.** `explorer/alidade_wave.mjs`. The identity is checked at 200,000
sampled cells for each of `P = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32`: **0 disagreements** inside the
wedge `k < K_n` in every case, and 49.9–50.1% disagreement outside it — chance,
as it should be. The first appearance of each period is confirmed from the
recurrence alone: `1@0 2@3 4@8 8@29 16@400 32@87867`. And the prediction the
dictionary makes is checked against an independent measurement: the front should
leave the period-16 domain at diagonal 87,867, around row `87867/0.757 ≈ 116,073`;
the previous sighting measured the front's jump over `κ = 87,867` at row 117,324.
To falsify: find a cell inside a wedge where the identity fails, or a doubling
diagonal not in the list.

**What it would give.** A precise statement of why this project had to compute the
background diagonal by diagonal instead of inferring it: the domain is a
travelling wave whose period is unbounded, so the literature's inference step
(*"the identification of domains begins with inference of FAs from examples of the
CA's behavior i.e., the discovery of patterns in space-time data. In simple cases
this can be done by inspection."*) cannot terminate. It also gives the shape of
the logarithmic period bound the previous sighting wanted for its run-length
argument: `K_n` grows roughly as squares, so the period at time `t` is about
`log t`. What remains: the growth of `K_n` is measured, not proved.

### 3.3 No domain filter can find the seam, because the two phases have the same row language

**The claim.** A Crutchfield–Hanson domain filter is a finite-state transducer
reading one row from left to right, and no such object can locate rule 30's seam,
because a row of the settled region and a row of the band are drawn from the same
language: every word of length 14 occurs in both, and their entropies differ by
0.0026 bits per cell. The project's `E = picture xor S` is a filter, but it is a
*two-dimensional* one that compares rows `2^n` apart, and nothing one-dimensional
replaces it.

**The dictionary.**

| Here | Computational mechanics |
|---|---|
| a row of the settled picture | a configuration in the domain `Λ` |
| a row inside the band | a configuration to be filtered |
| a word absent from `Λ` but present in the band | a **wall**: *"We consider a domain A and a finite string ω = zs such that z ∈ A, s ∉ A, and ω ∉ A. Then s is a wall of domain A"* |
| the transducer's state | how much of the row must be read before a site can be classified (their "synchronization") |
| **Seam** | there are no such words. Over 5.5·10^8 length-14 windows of settled rows, **every** one of the 16384 words occurs, the rarest 8062 times; over 1.2·10^8 windows of band rows, likewise. The best any length-14 test could do is a word that is 1.96× more likely in one phase than the other |

**What it leans on.** The fetched wall definition above; nothing else external.

**The test.** `explorer/alidade_wordcount.mjs`, exhaustive over rows 5000–39999
for the settled phase (whole settled part of each row, 550,767,000 windows) and
rows 20000–39999 for the band (119,760,000 windows): 0 words of length 14 absent
from either; settled `H(14)/14 = 0.99743` bits per cell, band `0.99999`; black
densities 0.49994 and 0.49996; the most over-represented settled word is at
1.964× the band's rate and the most under-represented at 0.246×. To falsify:
exhibit a word absent from the settled phase and present in the band. (I thought I
had 26 of them; §4 records why that was wrong, because the way it was wrong is the
useful part.)

**What it would give.** It closes the whole "build a filter and read off the
particles" family in one measurement, and it explains the previous sighting's
fourth obstruction from a new direction: the settled region carries no trace of
the boundary *and* no trace of itself, to a finite-state reader of one row.

### 3.4 Not a defect gas: rule 18's particles thin, and rule 30's do not

**The claim.** The one elementary rule whose filtered dynamics is a gas of
annihilating particles is rule 18, and its defect density decays like `t^(-1/2)`;
rule 30's band has deviation density 1/2 at every depth and never thins, so there
is no dilute limit, no reaction rate, and no annihilating system for the front to
be the leftmost particle of. The front is a genuinely narrow wall — three cells —
but there is exactly one of it, and annihilation needs two.

**The dictionary.**

| Here | Rule 18's defect gas |
|---|---|
| the settled picture | the domain `(0Σ)*` |
| a cell of `E` | a defect site |
| the block `11` in a rule 18 row | the defect indicator |
| defect density against time | `t^(-0.527)` measured over 10^5 steps on a ring of 65536 |
| the band's deviation density against depth behind the front | 1.0 at the front, 0.4606 at depth 1, 0.5801 at depth 2, and 0.50005 averaged over depths 16 to 96 |
| a pair annihilation | 68% of last-transient deaths in `explorer/maskfront.mjs` are two transients meeting in one `\|\|` |
| **Seam 1** | there is no dilute limit. At density 1/2 the "particles" are touching everywhere, so the mean free path is one cell and the gas has no kinetics |
| **Seam 2** | the paper's particle needs *"the width of the defect never exceeds some fixed maximum"*. The front's leading block has mean length 1.93 and a geometric tail — 0.5378, 0.2388, 0.1113, 0.0511, … out to 12 and beyond — with no cutoff visible over 10^6 rows |
| **Seam 3** | and it needs temporal periodicity, which would force a rational velocity with denominator dividing the domain's period. The measured velocity is 0.243 and the domain's period changes for ever (§3.2) |

**What it leans on.** For rule 18 the fetched sentence — *"the filtered behavior
is described by a stochastic equation of motion for diffusive annihilating
particles"* ([ECA54.pdf](https://csc.ucdavis.edu/~cmg/papers/ECA54.pdf)) — and
then, rather than a citation for the exponent, a measurement. **UNVERIFIED**: the
primary sources for rule 18's kink, Crutchfield & Hanson's *Turbulent pattern
bases for cellular automata* (Physica D 69, 1993) and Eloranta & Nummelin's *The
kink of cellular automaton rule 18 performs a random walk* (J. Stat. Phys. 69,
1992). Searched and fetched: `csc.ucdavis.edu/~cmg/papers/TurBases.pdf` downloads
but contains no text layer at all (0 characters recovered by the same extractor
that got 91,000 from ECA54.pdf — it is a scan);
`link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01058766` returns 303 to an
`idp.springer.com/authorize` endpoint. So the `t^(-1/2)` law is asserted here on
the strength of my own measurement of rule 18, not on either paper.

**The test.** `explorer/alidade_rule18.mjs`: rule 18 on a ring of 65536 from a
fixed random row, density of the block `11` sampled at log-spaced times, fitted
exponent **−0.5272** over `t ≥ 1000`. Rule 30's profile is from
`explorer/alidade_survival.mjs` over 10^6 rows. To falsify: find a depth behind
rule 30's front at which the deviation density is measurably below 1/2, or a
filtering of the band under which it decays.

**What it would give.** Nothing positive; it removes the vantage's most attractive
hypothesis. Its value is that the removal is measured rather than argued, and that
the same measurement pins down what *is* true of the front — it is narrow, and its
narrowness is the reason the survival law of §3.1 has only three cells in it.

### 3.5 The residual in the complexity–entropy plane, and why this field has no theorem there

**The claim.** Computational mechanics scores a process by entropy rate `h` and
statistical complexity `C_μ`; "eventually periodic with period `p`" is the corner
`h = 0`, `C_μ = log p`, and the centre column measures `h ≈ 1`, `C_μ ≈ 0`, which
is the *opposite* corner and is also where a fair coin sits. So the field's own
coordinates place the residual as far from periodicity as a sequence can be, and
supply nothing that converts the measurement into the conclusion — because both
coordinates are defined over an ensemble and here there is one orbit.

**The dictionary.**

| Here | Computational mechanics |
|---|---|
| the centre column | a binary process |
| "eventually periodic with period `p`" | `h = 0` and `C_μ = log₂ p`: `p` causal states in one cycle |
| the measured block entropies | `h(14) = 0.99008` bits per symbol over 6·10^5 terms |
| the causal states at horizon 4 and 6 | exactly **one**: every past of length 4 or 6 is followed by all 2^8 futures |
| crystal 21 and Talus's factor counts | the deterministic surrogate for a causal-state count, and the one that actually bounds a period |
| **Seam 1** | `C_μ` cannot separate the two hypotheses: a fair coin and this sequence both give one causal state, and so would the *first half* of a period-10^9 sequence. Only `h` separates, and `h` is not computable from any finite prefix |
| **Seam 2** | the plug-in entropy estimator is biased downward once the block length approaches `log₂` of the sample size. Measured `h(n)` falls to 0.13 by `n = 22` on 6·10^5 terms, and that is the estimator, not the sequence. Any argument of the form "the measured entropy is 1, so it is not periodic" is exactly this error with the sign hidden |

**What it leans on.** Nothing external that I could fetch; the definitions of `h`
and `C_μ` are standard in this literature and the fetched paper uses ε-machine
reconstruction without restating them. **UNVERIFIED** for the formal definitions
of statistical complexity and the ε-machine: searched for Crutchfield & Young and
for Shalizi & Crutchfield, *Computational mechanics: pattern and prediction,
structure and simplicity*; the Springer landing page is the only fetchable form
and it redirects to authorisation.

**The test.** `explorer/alidade_epsilon.mjs`, 6·10^5 terms of the centre column:
all 2^n words present up to `n = 15`, `h(14) = 0.99008`, one causal state at past
lengths 4 and 6 with futures of length 8. Reported with the caveat above: at past
length 8 the script finds 7 follower sets, which is a sample-size artefact of the
same kind and should not be read as structure.

**What it would give.** A clean restatement of the residual for a reader from this
field, and one honest warning: the field's headline diagram would place rule 30's
centre column at (1, 0) with confidence, and that placement is a measurement of a
prefix and proves nothing at all.

## 4. Died in translation

- **The vantage's own hypothesis: the front as the leftmost particle of an
  annihilating gas.** Dead at the density. Rule 18's defects thin as `t^(-0.527)`
  (measured); rule 30's band sits at 0.50005 at every depth from 16 to 96 cells
  behind the front and at 0.4987 at depth 3. A gas needs a dilute limit and there
  is none. The *question* the vantage carried — bound the death rate from the
  domain — survived and paid; the *mechanism* did not.
- **The reaction table as a source of the death rate.** The brief pointed at
  `explorer/maskfront.mjs`'s kill types (two transients meeting in a single `||`
  at 68%, a black settled neighbour at 4%) as the analogue of a CM reaction table,
  and I spent an hour expecting the front's deaths to be 96% band-internal. They
  are not. That table is about the death of the last transient *of a diagonal*,
  which is a different event from a retreat of the front; at the front the fate is
  decided by the background alone on 76.9% of rows and 50.1% of retreats are
  domain-forced. Naming what a number was measured over would have saved the hour.
- **The greedy walker using the forced-retreat rule.** The obvious way to turn the
  survival law into a bound: advance on white, retreat by one on the forcing
  triple, otherwise stay. It runs at 0.942 and sits *left* of the real front on 13
  of 300,000 rows, because the forcing triple is only meaningful at the true front.
  The rule has to be carried by a reachable *set*, not a point; that is §3.1 and
  the difference between the two is the whole result.
- **Twenty-six forbidden words that were not forbidden.** A first pass
  (`explorer/alidade_gap.mjs`, 1.6·10^8 sampled cells) found 26 words of length 14
  absent from the settled phase and present ~2900 times each in the band — which
  would have meant a domain filter exists. It is a sampling artefact, and the cause
  is §3.2: in the period-16 regime the settled picture is a travelling wave with
  `S(t+16, x−16) = S(t, x)`, so rows 16 apart are the same row shifted and a sample
  that steps `t` by 4 sees only a quarter of the phases, however many cells it
  touches. An exhaustive count over every row (`explorer/alidade_wordcount.mjs`,
  5.5·10^8 windows) finds all 16384 words, the rarest 8062 times. Recorded at
  length because it is the project's own recurring failure: 1.6·10^8 was a true
  number measured over the wrong thing, and the shortfall was far too large to be
  chance, which made it *more* convincing rather than less.
- **ε-machine reconstruction as the way to find the domain.** The literature's
  inference step reads space-time data and infers a finite automaton. It would
  never find rule 30's domain: the two phases have the same row language (§3.3),
  and the domain's own period is unbounded, so there is no finite automaton to
  infer. The domain here was found by the project along diagonals, which is not a
  direction this literature reads in.
- **The full shift as the domain.** Rule 30 is surjective (`schule-stoop-2012`
  Prop. 15), so `{0,1}^ℤ` satisfies both conditions of the definition trivially and
  *is* a regular domain of rule 30 with period 1. Its filter flags nothing. This is
  not a joke row: it is why "does rule 30 have a regular domain" is the wrong
  question, and "does it have one that excludes the band" is the right one.
- **Particle identification and a glider catalogue.** Rule 54 has a catalogue with
  velocities and a reaction table; rule 110's catalogue carries a universality
  proof. Rule 30's picture contains exactly one wall and no gliders, so there is
  nothing to catalogue. Died on inspection.
- **Cellular transducers.** The literature's own escape hatch for CAs whose
  filtered behaviour is not finite-state. The class is named in the fetched source
  and carries, so far as I could find, no theorems that bound anything. An address,
  not a route.
- **Shock waves and a Rankine–Hugoniot condition for the seam speed.** The
  attraction: a shock's velocity is fixed by the jump in a conserved density across
  it, which would give 0.243 in closed form. There is no conserved density (rule 30
  is not additive), and the obvious candidate — entropy density — does not jump:
  0.99743 bits per cell on the settled side against 0.99999 on the band side.
- **Toom's eroder theory.** The retreats are erosion and Toom's theorem computes
  erosion rates, but every result there needs monotonicity, and rule 30 is
  left-permutive: flipping the left input flips the output, so no configuration
  order is preserved. Died in one line.
- **Dislocations and Burgers vectors.** The eventually-white diagonals, where the
  settled period doubles and one bit is chosen, look exactly like dislocations with
  a topological charge; and the project even knows the chosen bits
  (`explorer/forbit.mjs`). But the charge is not conserved, not additive, and is
  inherited unchanged by every configuration white far to the left, so there is
  nothing for a topological argument to be about.
- **Statistical complexity as a discriminator.** `C_μ` is small for a fair coin and
  small for a short-period sequence; only the entropy rate separates them, and no
  finite prefix determines it. The field's most-used number is blind to exactly the
  distinction the residual is about.

## 5. What to hand the theorist

**Topic 1 — the survival law, and the reachable-set bound below 1/2.** This is the
whole document.

*The claim to falsify, in three pieces, smallest first.*
(a) *The law.* For rows `c` (the picture) and `d` (the settled picture) with
`c (i-1) = d (i-1)` and `c i = ! d i`,
`xor (rule30 c i) (rule30 d i) = xor (! d (i+1)) (d i && xor (c (i+1)) (d (i+1)))`.
Already proved in the kernel, `explorer/alidade_scratch_survival.lean`, axioms
`[propext]`, together with the two corollaries that make the right-hand side
`! d (i+1)` when `d i = false` or when `c (i+1) = d (i+1)`. This is a seedable node
of size S sitting under `leftDiagonal_onset_le`, and it generalises crystal 50(b),
which is its `c (i+1) = d (i+1)` half in diagonal coordinates.
(b) *The forced retreat.* If `S(t, F(t)−1)` is black, `S(t, F(t))` white and
`S(t, F(t)+1)` black, then `F(t+1) > F(t)`. Immediate from (a) plus crystals A2.
Measured on 132,152 of 999,960 rows with no exception.
(c) *The bound.* Let `R(t₀) = {F(t₀)}` and let `R(t+1)` be the image of `R(t)`
under `x ↦ {x−1}` when `S(t,x−1)` is white, `{x}` when the triple is `(1,0,0)`,
`[x+1,∞)` when it is `(1,0,1)` and `[x,∞)` otherwise. Then `F(t) ≥ min R(t)` for
every `t ≥ t₀`. That is a one-step induction from (a) and A2 and is the statement
worth a session; the data structure in `explorer/alidade_dp2.mjs` is only the
observation that `R(t)` is always a finite set plus an upward ray.

*The dictionary row it depends on:* "the domain-forced retreat is a decay channel
whose rate the domain computes" — and, more sharply, the row that says the
mechanism is a *gap in the reachable set*, not a slow walker.

*The depth that would settle it.* `min R(t)` runs at 0.45310 over 4·10^6 rows on
the channel-free stretch from diagonal 100,000, with every 5·10^5-block in
`[0.45265, 0.45412]`; the same code gives 0.45149 on pseudo-random bits, 0.45029
on phase-randomised settled words and 0.45292 on the evolution of a random ring.
The real front is never left of `min R(t)` over 300,000 rows with the engine
running alongside. What is *not* settled and is the honest gap: nothing proves the
DP's speed stays below 1/2 on every stretch, and the DP escapes onto the
eventually-white diagonals exactly as Rosetta's `G` does, so the stretches must be
chained through Rosetta's Topic 2. Both gaps are the same shape as the ones the
previous sighting left, with one difference that decides whether this is worth a
session: its margin was 0.001 and against it, this one is 0.047 and for it.

**Topic 2 — the prerequisite, which is already on the previous sighting's list.**
*The front never rides a white channel:* for every `t`, the settled word
`S_{κ(t)−1}` is not identically white. Two lines from `leftDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow`
and A2. It was worth a session before; it is now load-bearing, because without it
Topic 1's bound covers only the stretch between two doublings and there is no
argument that tiles all of time.

**Not handed over.** §3.2's domain hierarchy and §3.3's row-language measurement
are descriptions, not routes: they say why the CM programme cannot be run on rule
30 and why the project's own diagonal construction was the only way in. A captain
who wants an obstruction out of this document should take §3.3 — *no finite-state
